# Brief: take over the grant reporting, and make it survivable

Grant reporting has been done by one person for six years and she leaves at the
end of March. Nothing is documented. The reports have always been on time and
correct, which has meant nobody has ever had a reason to look at how they are
produced, and now we have about ten weeks to find out.

This is a handover brief and a rebuild brief at the same time, and the handover
part is urgent.

## What we know

There are seven funders on different reporting cycles. Two are quarterly, four
are annual, one is on a schedule tied to project milestones that nobody but her
appears to understand. Each has its own template, its own definition of eligible
expenditure, and its own tolerance for restating a previously reported figure.

The reports are assembled from the finance system, the project time records, and
a set of spreadsheets she maintains. The spreadsheets are the part I am worried
about. They are on her drive, they cross-reference each other, and at least one
of them contains figures that are not derivable from any system — they are
judgements she made and recorded.

There is no test of correctness other than that the funders have not complained.

## Priorities, in order

1. Get everything off her personal drive and into the shared one, this week,
   before anything else. Whatever else goes wrong, we should not lose the files.
2. Sit with her and watch a full cycle. The two quarterly funders both report in
   February, which is fortunate — that is the last full cycle before she goes and
   it should be treated as the primary handover event.
3. Write down what she does, in enough detail that a competent person who has
   never seen it could do it. Not a summary. The failure mode here is a document
   that describes the process at a level of abstraction that is useless in front
   of the actual spreadsheet.
4. Identify the judgements. Every figure that is not derivable from a system is a
   judgement, and each one needs its basis recorded while she is still here to
   explain it. This is the part that becomes unrecoverable in April.
5. Only then think about improving it. The temptation will be to redesign as you
   learn, and it will cost you the handover.

## The milestone-linked funder

Deal with this one first among the seven. It is the one with the least
predictable schedule, the one where she is the only person who has ever spoken
to the funder's contact, and the one where a missed report has a contractual
consequence rather than an apologetic email.

Get introduced to their contact before she leaves. An introduction from her is
worth six months of building a relationship from nothing.

## After March

Once the handover is secure, I want a view on whether this should stay as one
person's job. My instinct is that it should not — the concentration of knowledge
is exactly what has put us in this position — but splitting it across three
people who each do it twice a year has its own obvious failure mode. Give me
your view with the reasoning, not a survey of options.

## What success looks like

In April, a report goes out on time and correct, produced by someone who is not
her, from a written process, with the judgements documented. That is the whole
goal. Everything else is secondary to it.

## Practicalities

She is generous with her time and she is also still doing the day job, so the
handover competes with the February cycle for her attention. Book the time in
her calendar now, in blocks, rather than assuming you can catch her.

Do not record the sessions. She has said she would rather not be, and a
handover where the person is guarded is worse than one where you have to take
notes by hand.

Copy me on the written process as it develops rather than at the end. I will
know when a section is thinner than the thing it describes, and it is much
cheaper to say so in February than in April.

## One more risk

There is a chance the spreadsheets contain an error that has been carried
forward for years and never caught, because the only check on correctness is
that nobody complained. If you find one, tell me before you tell anyone else,
and do not correct it in the middle of the handover. Restating a previously
reported figure is a conversation with a funder, not a spreadsheet edit.
